title: (Scenario) A Kafka topic has a hot partition due to skewed key distribution (e.g. one enterprise customer generates 80% of traffic) — how do you fix it without downtime: increasing partitions helps spread NON-skewed traffic but the same key still maps deterministically to one partition (hash(key) % numPartitions), so the real fix is key bucketing/salting (e.g. key = customerId + "-" + hash(orderId) % 4) to split one logical key across multiple partitions — and what is the consumer-side trade-off (must read from multiple partitions and merge results for that customer)?
shortTitle: (Scenario) A Kafka topic has a hot partition due to a skewed key — how do you fix it without downtime, and what is the consumer-side trade-off?

s1_definition.profdef: A hot partition occurs when one key, or a small set of keys, receives a disproportionate share of traffic, so the partition that key maps to becomes a bottleneck while other partitions sit idle. Because Kafka assigns a keyed record to a partition with the deterministic formula hash of the key modulo the number of partitions, a single high-volume key always lands on one partition, and simply adding partitions does not help that key, it only spreads the other, non-skewed keys. The real fix is key bucketing or salting: you augment the key with a bucket suffix so one logical key is split across several physical keys and therefore several partitions. The trade-off is on the consumer side, which must now read all the buckets for that logical key and merge them, giving up strict single-partition ordering for the split key.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sorts incoming transfer slips into counters by customer, so each customer's slips always go to the same counter to keep them in order. One enterprise customer sends eighty percent of all slips, so that one counter is swamped while the others are nearly empty. Adding more counters does not help, because the rule still sends all of that giant customer's slips to the same single counter. The fix is to split that one customer into several sub-queues, for example "BigCorp line 1," "BigCorp line 2," "BigCorp line 3," and "BigCorp line 4," by tagging each slip with a sub-line number derived from the order number, so four counters now share the load. The cost is that if you later want the full picture for BigCorp, you must gather slips from all four sub-lines and merge them, because they are no longer in one neat ordered pile.
s1_definition.oneliner: Adding partitions cannot relieve a single hot key because hash(key) mod partitions is deterministic; split the hot key with a bucket suffix so it spans multiple partitions, and accept that consumers must read and merge across those buckets, losing strict per-logical-key ordering.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A hot partition occurs when one key, or a small set of keys, receives a disproportionate share of traffic, so the partition that key maps to becomes a bottleneck while other partitions sit idle. Because Kafka assigns a keyed record to a partition with the deterministic formula hash of the key modulo the number of partitions, a single high-volume key always lands on one partition, and simply adding partitions does not help that key, it only spreads the other, non-skewed keys. The real fix is key bucketing or salting: you augment the key with a bucket suffix so one logical key is split across several physical keys and therefore several partitions. The trade-off is on the consumer side, which must now read all the buckets for that logical key and merge them, giving up strict single-partition ordering for the split key.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India sorts incoming transfer slips into counters by customer, so each customer's slips always go to the same counter to keep them in order. One enterprise customer sends eighty percent of all slips, so that one counter is swamped while the others are nearly empty. Adding more counters does not help, because the rule still sends all of that giant customer's slips to the same single counter. The fix is to split that one customer into several sub-queues, for example "BigCorp line 1," "BigCorp line 2," "BigCorp line 3," and "BigCorp line 4," by tagging each slip with a sub-line number derived from the order number, so four counters now share the load. The cost is that if you later want the full picture for BigCorp, you must gather slips from all four sub-lines and merge them, because they are no longer in one neat ordered pile.

**One line to remember:** Adding partitions cannot relieve a single hot key because hash(key) mod partitions is deterministic; split the hot key with a bucket suffix so it spans multiple partitions, and accept that consumers must read and merge across those buckets, losing strict per-logical-key ordering.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with why the obvious fix fails. When you key a record, the partitioner computes hash of the key modulo the number of partitions. For one specific key, that formula yields exactly one partition number regardless of how many partitions exist. If you increase partitions from six to twelve, the hot key might move to a different single partition, but it is still confined to one partition, so its partition is still hot. Adding partitions genuinely helps the other keys, because their collective load now spreads across more partitions, but it does nothing for the concentration caused by one dominant key. This is the crux the question is testing.

The real fix is to change the key itself so the hot logical entity no longer maps to a single partition. This is key bucketing, also called salting. You pick a bucket count, say four, and derive a bucket from some varying field of the record, then append it to the key. For example the physical key becomes customerId plus a dash plus the hash of the orderId modulo four, so BigCorp's traffic is split into BigCorp-0, BigCorp-1, BigCorp-2, and BigCorp-3. Those four physical keys hash to up to four different partitions, so the load that was crushing one partition is now shared. You choose the bucket field so it varies within the hot entity, orderId or a timestamp component works well, and you choose the bucket count based on how much you need to spread; it does not need to equal the partition count, it just needs to be large enough to break the concentration.

Here is the producer-side code that implements the split:

```java
int buckets = 4; // split factor for hot customers
String physicalKey = customerId + "-" + (Integer.toString(orderId.hashCode() & 0x7fffffff)
        .hashCode() & 0x7fffffff) % buckets;
// simpler and clearer:
int bucket = Math.floorMod(orderId.hashCode(), buckets);
String key = customerId + "-" + bucket; // BigCorp-0 .. BigCorp-3
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders", key, payload));
```

A refinement used in practice is selective salting: you only split keys that are actually hot, leaving normal customers with their plain customerId key so you do not pay the merge cost for everyone. You maintain a small set of known hot keys, or detect them dynamically, and salt only those. This keeps ordering intact for the ninety-nine percent of customers that are not hot, and only the genuinely hot customer pays the trade-off.

Now the consumer-side trade-off, which is the second half of the question. Before salting, all of a customer's records were in one partition, so a single consumer read them in strict offset order, which gave you per-customer ordering for free. After salting, the hot customer's records are spread across several partitions, possibly handled by several consumers in the group. So you lose the automatic strict ordering for that customer, and if you need a complete or ordered view of that customer, the consumer side must read from all the relevant buckets and merge the results, for example by buffering and sorting on a sequence number or timestamp, or by having a downstream aggregation step that reassembles per-customer state. You must also decide whether strict ordering for the hot key still matters; often for a high-volume enterprise customer you only need ordering within an order, not across all their orders, in which case salting by orderId preserves exactly the ordering you actually need, because each individual order still lands in one bucket. The craft is picking the bucket field so that the ordering you must keep stays within a single bucket while the load you must spread crosses buckets.

Doing this without downtime is the final requirement. You cannot retroactively re-key existing data, so you roll it out going forward. You deploy the new partitioning logic behind a feature flag or configuration so producers start emitting salted keys for the hot entity, you update consumers first to understand both the old plain keys and the new salted keys and to merge across buckets, and then you flip producers. Because consumers already handle both key shapes, there is no gap and no downtime, and old in-flight records under the plain key drain naturally. If you also need more partitions for the non-skewed traffic, you add them as a separate, carefully planned change, mindful of the key-remapping caveat that repartitioning carries.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India publishes corporate payment orders to the `corp.orders` topic, keyed by customer id so each corporate client's orders stay ordered. One enterprise client, BigCorp, generates eighty percent of all orders. Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) are ordinary clients with light traffic.

Problem 1 — the partition that BigCorp hashes to is saturated: its consumer is perpetually behind while the partitions for ordinary clients are nearly idle. An engineer doubled the partitions and nothing improved for BigCorp. This is exactly the deterministic-mapping problem: BigCorp's single key still lands on one partition no matter how many partitions exist.

Problem 2 — we need to spread BigCorp's load without downtime and without scrambling the ordering that actually matters, which is the ordering of events within a single payment order. This is why we salt by order id, so each order stays in one bucket but BigCorp's many orders spread across buckets, and why consumers must merge across buckets for a full BigCorp view.

Our runnable demo models a `Partitioner`, publishes a skewed workload first with plain keys to show the hot partition, then with selective salting on the hot key to show the balanced spread, and finally a `MergingConsumer` that reads all BigCorp buckets and reassembles per-order ordering. The classes are `HotPartitionDemo`, `Partitioner`, `SaltingKeyStrategy`, `PartitionLoad`, and `MergingConsumer`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: ten thousand corporate orders where BigCorp produces eight thousand and fifty ordinary customers share two thousand, on a six-partition topic.

Step 1: With plain keys, every BigCorp order is keyed BIGCORP, which hashes to exactly one partition. That partition receives roughly eight thousand records while the other five partitions share only two thousand. The BigCorp partition is hot and its consumer falls behind.

Step 2: An engineer adds partitions. BigCorp's single key now hashes to some single partition out of the larger set, but it is still just one partition, so the hot spot moves but does not disappear. Only the non-skewed customers benefit from the extra partitions.

Step 3: We enable selective salting for BIGCORP with four buckets, salting by order id. Each BigCorp order is keyed BIGCORP-0 through BIGCORP-3 depending on the order id. These four physical keys hash to up to four partitions, so BigCorp's eight thousand orders spread across several partitions and no single partition is hot. Ordinary customers keep their plain keys and their strict ordering.

Step 4: Because each individual order's events share the same order id, they still land in the same bucket, so order-level ordering is preserved, which is the ordering that actually matters for payments. What is given up is strict ordering across all of BigCorp's orders, which we did not need.

Step 5: A downstream consumer that wants a complete ordered view of BigCorp now reads all four buckets and merges them by a producer-stamped sequence number, reassembling the combined sequence. This is the consumer-side trade-off: more partitions and keys to read, plus a merge step, in exchange for eliminating the hot partition without downtime.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A hot partition from a skewed key happens because Kafka assigns a keyed record with the deterministic formula hash of the key modulo the number of partitions. If one enterprise customer produces eighty percent of the traffic, that single key always hashes to one partition, so that partition is overwhelmed while the rest sit nearly idle. The first instinct is to add partitions, and that is exactly the trap this question tests: adding partitions spreads the non-skewed traffic, but the dominant key is still one key, so it still maps to a single partition. The hot spot might move to a different partition, but it does not go away.

The real fix is to change the key so the hot logical entity no longer maps to one partition, which is key bucketing or salting. I pick a bucket count, say four, derive a bucket from a varying field such as the order id, and append it to the key, so the one customer BigCorp becomes BigCorp-0 through BigCorp-3. Those four physical keys hash to up to four partitions, so the load that was crushing one partition is now shared. In practice I salt selectively, only the keys that are actually hot, so ordinary customers keep their plain key and their strict per-customer ordering and pay no cost, and only the genuinely hot customer is split.

The deliberate detail is choosing the salt field so the ordering you must keep stays inside one bucket. On the National Bank of India corporate orders stream, what matters is ordering of events within a single payment order, not across all of BigCorp's orders, so I salt by order id. Every event for one order shares the order id and therefore the same bucket, so order-level ordering is preserved, while BigCorp's many different orders spread across buckets to kill the hot partition. The thing I consciously give up is strict ordering across all of BigCorp's orders, which we never needed.

That leads to the consumer-side trade-off, which is the second half of the answer. Before salting, all of a customer's records lived in one partition, so a single consumer read them in strict order for free. After salting, the hot customer's records are spread across several partitions and possibly several consumers, so to reconstruct a complete or ordered view of that customer the consumer must read all the buckets and merge them, typically by buffering and sorting on a producer-stamped sequence number. Finally, I do all of this without downtime by rolling out the new key logic going forward: I first deploy consumers that understand both the old plain keys and the new salted keys and can merge across buckets, then I flip the producers behind a feature flag, and the old plain-keyed records drain naturally with no gap. I never try to re-key existing data, because the fix is about new traffic, and I keep the hot-customer list in configuration so adding a newly hot customer is a config change rather than a code change.
